# 1. What is Quarto?
[Quarto][url-quarto] is a powerful tool for creating reproducible documents, presentations, and websites.
It supports a wide range of output formats (HTML, PDF, and Word, etc).
It can run R, Python (including Jupyter notebooks), and Julia code. In short,
it enables you to publish books, decks, websites, etc.

It's prefect for blogging/ technical writing which has numerious benefits in terms of career develpment:

* learning to writing is learning to think[^note-jp]
* it organize your own knowledge which helps you synthesize new ideas[^note-jh]
* become a source of dopamine for future self[^note-future-self]

[^note-future-self]: as [Chase Hughes defines discipline](https://youtu.be/EDMmGeisx3o?si=Rjb9PrRytpRo4GrG&t=80)
a price of writing can be thought of then as a stepping stone as you progress towards your higher goal
or advance in the field that you are writing about.
The act of writing about something, forces you to discover the gaps in your thinking.
The filling in of those gaps teaches you to really get a full grasp of the idea that you are writing about.
The act of having written, having produced something tangible, having manifested something from the
mental field into the physical, creates a small foundation for you to step on or fallback on.
[^note-jp]: [Jordan Peterson](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/CPY3dG9dcC8) propose picking
a hard problem and write about it. William Zinsser summerized this process even better in his book
[Writing to Learn](https://youtu.be/IsQUT9xRYSg?si=YsGyY-Dh7TJb04PM&t=185)
[^note-jh]: [Jeremy Howard](https://www.fast.ai/posts/2020-01-16-fast_template.html#you-should-blog)
made this case on why you should blog and Rachel Thomas (co-founder of FastAI) advocates writing as
[personal branding or even alternative to a degree](https://www.fast.ai/posts/2019-05-13-blogging-advice.html#related-posts)

[url-quarto]: https://quarto.org

**This website itself is built using Quarto**, and this guide shows how that is done in 3 simple steps!

## Installation
To install Quarto, you can use the following command:

```bash
pipx install quarto-cli # <1>
```
1. quarto is actually written in Pandoc but there's a python interface around it called [`quarto-cli`](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli-pypi)

or
```bash
brew install --cask quarto # <2>
```
2. if it's already installed, you could update with a `brew upgrade --cask quarto`, use `brew outdated --cask` first to check if there's a newer version available.

# 2. Creating a Website Project
The official [docs](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/) on how to create a website is actually pretty comprehensive, but there's the TLDR:

## Create
The following command will create a new directory for your project and setup the scaffolding for a simple website in the `my-awesome-site` directory:

```bash
quarto create project blog my-awesome-site # <1>
```
1. use this to setup a site with a blog built-in

or
```bash
quarto create project website my-awesome-site # <2>
```
2. use this if you are sure you want a website without a blog and wanna keep things nice and simple

## Blog
if you have used the `quarto create project blog` option [above](#create),
you can control the listing of your blogs in your `index.qmd` which will be a listing page[^note-listing-page]

[^note-listing-page]: see [here](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-blog.html#home-page) on how to configure it

## Render
While editing your website/ blog, you can run `quarto preview`[^note-preview] to preview your site in a browser.

[^note-preview]: it's great because the whole site's rendered
and you can see the changes being applied in real-time. However, for a blog with lots of
computational heavy pages, it might be better to use `quarto render` instead or
make sure your posts are [frozen](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-blog.html#freezing-posts)
by default in your `posts/_metadata.yml`

Or use `quarto render` which can give you more granular control.
You open the pages rendered in `docs`[^note-output-dir] manually to "preview" changes.
`quarto render` will render the whole site which you might not need to do everytime since it's time consuming.
You can instead render individual pages or sections of your site for example, just a blog post:

[^note-output-dir]: or whereever you configured your `output-dir` to be in your `_quarto.yaml`

```bash
quarto render blog/first_post.qmd
```

by default, Quarto will render the site to the `_site` directory but you should change that to `docs`
using the `output-dir` variable in your project configuration `_quarto.yaml`:

```{.yml filename="_quarto.yaml"}
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs # <1>

website:
  title: "My Super Awesome Site"
  favicon: favicon.ico # <6>
  navbar: # <2>
    logo: logo.png # <5>
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - about.qmd # <3>

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo # <4>
    css: styles.css
    toc: true
```
1. need this for Github Pages deployment later
2. more about setting up website nav [here](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-navigation.html)
3. an about page is create by default, here's a [detailed guide](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-about.html) on how to set it up.
4. these are the [available options for HTML themes](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html)
5. Optional: put your site's logo here, if you have one, which will appear in the navbar.
6. Optional: put your site's favicon here, if you have one.

# 3. Deploy to Github Pages
there are [three ways](https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html#overview) to deploy to
Github Pages but the [Render to `docs`](https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html#render-to-docs)
method is the simplest and my personal preference. Here's how to set it up step-by-step:

## create github repo
First create a new repository on Github, then add it as a remote:

```bash
cd my-awesome-site
git init
git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repository.git # <1>
git pull origin main # <2>
```
1. update this to whatever your repo's URL is
2. pull in things like README.md, .gitignore,LICENSE.md, etc.

## gitignore
optional but might be good idea to make sure that `_site`[^note-site-ignore] and `.quarto` are ignored:
```{.txt filename=".gitignore"}
/.quarto/
/_site/

# other items to ignore
...
```

[^note-site-ignore]: created during `quarto preview`, see more about ignoring output from
the official [documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html#ignoring-output)

## init commit
then just add and commit:
```bash
quarto render # <1>
touch .nojekyll # <2>
git add docs .gitignore .nojekyll # <3>
git commit -m "init commit"
git push origin main
```
1. this should create everything in `docs` per [above](#render)
2. tell Github Pages not to do additional processing of the site's content using Jekyll
3. this will only add the rendered html files, you of course have the optional to add other files

## configure github repo
finally, go to your Github repo's settings and enable Github Pages. Choose the `docs` folder as the source:

![Example Github Page settings](https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/images/gh-pages-docs-dir.png){#fig-example .lightbox}

And that's it, your site is live!

Going forward, as you add new content, you just simply:
```bash
quarto render
git add docs
git commit -m "add new content"
git push origin main
```
